articles.excerpt: Disclosure: I ran this study with an AI assistant (Claude), which wrote the code, did the analysis and drafted the paper. It also did the manual check of my fix heuristic, so that check is not an inde…
articles.body: Disclosure: I ran this study with an AI assistant (Claude), which wrote the code, did the analysis and drafted the paper. It also did the manual check of my fix heuristic, so that check is not an independent human review. Results are aggregate; no developer, repo or commit is named. This is observational: "associated with", never "causes". Question: are commits that disclose AI help (e.g. a Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer) reverted or followed by a bug-fix more often than comparable human-only commits? I wrote down the hypotheses and definitions before pulling any data. The short answer: no clear difference, but the study is too small to say much. Method in brief Public GitHub APIs only, through my own authenticated gh . No repo was cloned and no code was run.

articles.title: Lessons from Running AI Voice Calls at Scale
articles.excerpt: A chatbot request takes a few seconds. A phone call takes minutes, and during those minutes it holds a telephony connection, a speech-to-text stream, LLM calls and text-to-speech output, all of which…
articles.body: A chatbot request takes a few seconds. A phone call takes minutes, and during those minutes it holds a telephony connection, a speech-to-text stream, LLM calls and text-to-speech output, all of which have their own limits and failure modes. Here are the lessons that matter most once an AI voice system goes from a handful of test calls to thousands a day. 1. A call is a session, not a request Web backends are built around short requests. Voice calls are long-lived sessions with state: who's on the line, what's been said, which step of the conversation you're in. Keep that state outside the process handling the audio (Redis works well), so a worker restart or a reconnect doesn't lose the conversation. 2.

articles.title: Stave is the Substrate: Five Reasoning Paradigms on One Snapshot
articles.excerpt: ✓ Human-authored analysis; AI used for formatting and proofreading. AWS Compliance Mod is the canonical implementation of one Previous article Stave and the AWS Compliance Mod: why we ship both, makes…
articles.body: ✓ Human-authored analysis; AI used for formatting and proofreading. AWS Compliance Mod is the canonical implementation of one reasoning paradigm per-resource SQL benchmarks against framework requirements. Stave is the substrate. Five reasoning engines: SMT, Datalog, answer-set programming, Prolog, probabilistic model checking produce correct answers from Stave's exports without reading a line of Stave's source code. Previous article Stave and the AWS Compliance Mod: why we ship both , makes the per-feature complementarity argument: compound chain detection by Stave covers the compositional risk class that per-resource framework checks (AWS Compliance Mod) can't see by construction. That framing is still correct. Run both; they cover orthogonal territory.

articles.title: Testing AI Pipelines Without Calling the Model Every Time
articles.excerpt: Tests that call a real LLM are slow, cost money on every run, and fail randomly because the output changes. So many teams quietly skip testing their AI features altogether. The fix is to notice that m…
articles.body: Tests that call a real LLM are slow, cost money on every run, and fail randomly because the output changes. So many teams quietly skip testing their AI features altogether. The fix is to notice that most of an "AI pipeline" isn't the model at all. Building the prompt, retrieving context, parsing the reply and deciding what to do next are ordinary, deterministic code, and ordinary code is easy to test. 1. Put the model behind an interface Make your pipeline depend on a small interface instead of a specific SDK: from typing import Protocol class LLM ( Protocol ) : async def complete ( self , prompt : str ) -> str : . . . class FakeLLM : def __init__ ( self , reply : str ) -> None : self . reply = reply self .

articles.title: The 45-Minute Setup Problem: Why Your Dev Environment Is the Real Bottleneck in 2026
articles.excerpt: Originally published on tamiz.pro. You clone the repo at 9:00 AM. The clock starts. By the time you've installed the right Node version, spun up Postgres, wired the environment variables, pulled the m…
articles.body: Originally published on tamiz.pro . You clone the repo at 9:00 AM. The clock starts. By the time you've installed the right Node version, spun up Postgres, wired the environment variables, pulled the monorepo's 400 packages, and debugged the one missing system library, it's 9:45. You haven't written a line of code. This is the 45-minute setup problem, and in 2026, it's the single largest — and most under-acknowledged — bottleneck in the software development lifecycle. The 45-Minute Metric The number isn't pulled from thin air. For a mid-size microservice architecture or a monorepo with a polyglot toolchain, 45 minutes is a conservative median for a cold environment setup on a modern laptop.
articles.author: Tamiz Uddin

articles.title: AI Is Now Literally Frying Your Brain, And You Are Not Even Realising it
articles.excerpt: You can feel it happening in small, everyday moments. You stare at a blank email and feel the pull to let a chatbot write the first sentence. You finish a report with AI's help, and ten minutes later…
articles.body: You can feel it happening in small, everyday moments. You stare at a blank email and feel the pull to let a chatbot write the first sentence. You finish a report with AI's help, and ten minutes later you can barely remember what it said. People joke that AI is "frying our brains." New research from MIT, Wharton and leading medical journals suggests the joke is closer to a diagnosis than a meme. Relying heavily on AI is weakening memory, dulling instincts and training our minds to switch off. Convenience was always going to have a cost. We just didn't expect to pay it in thinking. AI doesn't need to damage brain tissue to leave us mentally sluggish. It works more like a cast on a healthy limb.

articles.title: Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured
articles.excerpt: An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity, and that verifies Einstein's greatest theory.
articles.body: An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity , which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like. Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image shows the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away. The image of this black hole , designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all?

articles.title: Voyager 1 team, unbowed by communications glitch, celebrates epic 1-light-day distance milestone
articles.excerpt: The Voyager 1 team celebrated the probe's big distance milestone on Thursday (Nov. 19), even while dealing with a communication anomaly that recently cropped up on the probe.
articles.body: PASADENA, Calif. – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov. 19), celebrating a big milestone — Voyager 1 just reached one light-day from Earth , something no other spacecraft has ever done. The excitement persisted despite a communication anomaly that cropped up on the probe, which the team remains confident is temporary. Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2 , flew past Neptune.
